# Norn test vectors

This directory is the **cross-implementation contract** (`SPEC.md` §12). A
second implementation that reproduces everything here agrees with Norn on every
byte that matters, and one that does not has found either a bug or a hole in
the specification — both of which are worth knowing.

Nothing here needs this repository. The files are plain CBOR, JSON, text and
`tlog-tiles` directories, and `SPEC.md` beside them is the only document *of
this project* required to interpret any of it.

It is not self-contained, and says so: §16.2 states plainly that "a reader who
does not fetch BIP-350 cannot implement this section", and §8.1 and §11.1 defer
their proof algorithms to RFC 6962 rather than restating them. The preamble
lists every such dependency. `SPEC.md` tells you what Norn decides; the
standards it names tell you what it reuses.

## Provenance — three, stated plainly

A vector proves a format, not a fact about the world, and how much it proves
depends on who wrote the bytes.

| Produced by | What | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **`contrib/norn-ref`** (the Python reference) | entries, state, trust, enrollment requests | Written from `SPEC.md` by a second implementation; the Go code must match them, not the other way round |
| **`cmd/norn-genlog`** (this project's Go) | `served/`, `served-large/`, `proofs/`, `fork/`, `checkpoints-bad/` | Producing a tiled log requires a log. Validated against libraries neither implementation wrote: `transparency-dev/formats` parses the checkpoint and `x/mod/sumdb/tlog` checks every inclusion proof |
| **`python-opentimestamps`** (the OTS reference) | `anchors/` | Norn reads `.ots` files and never writes them, so the suite's copies come from the implementation that owns the format |

Regenerate the first two with `make vectors` and `make vectors-log`. The third
is never regenerated — see `contrib/ots-vector/`, and the reason is the point
of having it.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `keys.json` | every test key: Ed25519 `{seed, public, kid}` by name, X25519 public keys, and `net` |
| `entries/` | one valid entry per type, canonical bytes, each with a `.json` mirror carrying its hashes and preimage |
| `log/` | the 159-entry replay fixture. **Read the order from `manifest.json`**, never by sorting filenames; entries that must be refused carry a `.reason` file. `51-enroll-unicode-labels` is accepted with malformed reserved hints and preserves them in `state.json`. `133-bad-root_add-counts-its-own-key` is the §4.2 case: a `root_add` signed by two of three roots and by the key in its own body, which is `threshold` because signatures resolve against the state BEFORE the entry |
| `state.json` | the state those 159 entries replay to, in canonical JSON (§14) |
| `proven/` | the devices a node admits at four evaluation times, including the boundary where `expires == T`, and under `grants` each active device's §4.0 grant (D-073). `state.json` is clock-independent on purpose, so this is the only vector that exercises expiry — the rule that decides when a device stops being admitted |
| `entries-hostile/` | input the profile must refuse: the eight `bare-` cases are one banned item each — null, undefined, float, negative integer, tag, indefinite length, a non-text map key and invalid UTF-8 — with no schema above them, so only the profile can refuse. The rest are input at and past §4.0's three resource limits — the entry size, the nesting depth and the map-key cap. A case with `says` must be refused for that reason; one marked `accepted` sits exactly at a limit and must be accepted, which is what bounds the limit from below |
| `genesis/` | twenty ways a genesis entry is refused. `18` and `19` are step 7's two halves — the **role** a signature declares and the **key set** it resolves against; `20` is a `name` one byte past the 64-byte cap |
| `genesis-good/` | geneses a reader MUST accept, one single-entry log each with the state it replays to: `01-name-at-the-cap`, a `name` of exactly 64 bytes in two-byte characters. The other side of `genesis/`'s name bound |
| `trust.cbor`, `trust.toml`, `trust.fingerprint` | the anchor in both encodings, and the fingerprint an operator compares out of band (§9.3) |
| `log-empty/` | a log with no entries at all, and the zero state §5.1 says it replays to. A reader that treats no genesis as a missing one reports `bad-genesis` instead |
| `trust-good/` | trust files §9.1 **permits**: a witness with no `url`, an `anchor` whose `type` this version does not know, opaque and mismatched URL strings, a present empty witness URL, and `at-the-cap`, exactly `MAX_TRUST_BYTES` long (`trust-bad/41-one-past-the-cap` is the same file one byte longer). Only a positive shows these values must be accepted |
| `trust-bad/` | 42 anchors that must be rejected. `07` and `08` isolate the no-witness and duplicate-name rules; `13`, `42` and `43` isolate derived-origin equality, witness-key correspondence and the closed-anchor rule. `40` is the log-key name plus one character, so only equality refuses it. `37` and `39` change one declared key ID, in the log key and a witness key, and carry that key into the policy too so only recomputation refuses them. `44-log-key-base64-cr` leaves the key bytes unchanged and is refused because its base64 data contains a carriage return |
| `policies/` | SPEC §9.1's C2SP `tlog-policy` grammar. `cases.json` says which whole policies MUST parse or MUST be refused, and why; `evaluate` tables pin what each quorum means. The files are byte-exact: every directive, including the last, needs a line feed. Cases cover quorum ordering, reserved names, verifier-key IDs and algorithms, duplicate public keys across vkey aliases and directive types, threshold bounds, CRLF, and forbidden ASCII controls (including controls hidden inside comments). Non-ASCII whitespace such as U+00A0 and U+0085 remains content. `two-log-lines` is accepted because its keys differ; the aliases are refused because their underlying public keys match |
| `requests/`, `requests-bad/` | enrollment requests (§16), including signed 203-byte padding and 256-byte label controls, accepted malformed `ip`/`endpoint` hints, and 25 refusals across all four layers. Each positive case carries a `form`: `canonical` for §16.2's lowercase text, or `uppercase` for the same request in the form §16.2 says a reader MUST also accept |
| `receipt.note`, `receipt.json` | a submission receipt (§7) and its parsed form |
| `receipt-bad/` | sixteen receipts that MUST be refused, covering all eight closed §7 codes. `cases.json` ties each code to the rule of the step that decides it. Body and signer negatives are re-signed; `leaf-hash-nonzero-pad-bits.note` changes only unused pad bits and decodes to the good receipt's leaf hash, and `leaf-hash-unpadded.note` drops its `=`. The six `order-` cases each fail two adjacent §7 steps and MUST be refused for the earlier: they are what holds the order. The extra-final-newline note-framing case cannot be re-signed, and the expired cases give their checking time explicitly |
| `served/` | the log as a static site: `checkpoint`, entry bundles and hash tiles |
| `checkpoints-bad/` | thirty checkpoints that MUST be refused. `cases.json`'s `rules` map names, for each, the SPEC section that states the rule it is about and a phrase that appears there — so a negative cannot exist without the rule being written where a reader will look, each served in place of `served/checkpoint` over the honest tiles. `cases.json` says what each one is, and its `codes` map names the SPEC §10.1 code each MUST be refused with — the first step that fails decides, so `01-unsigned` is `note` and not `log-signature`, and `03-wrong-origin` (signed under another origin's name) is `log-signature` and not `origin`. `checkpoints-bad/25-signature-nonzero-pad-bits`, `checkpoints-bad/26-cosignature-nonzero-pad-bits` and `checkpoints-bad/27-root-nonzero-pad-bits` change only unused base64 pad bits while keeping decoded signatures or roots unchanged. `checkpoints-bad/29-root-unpadded` drops the root's `=`, which a lenient decoder reads as the same 32 bytes, and `checkpoints-bad/30-noncanonical-size-under-untrusted-signer` fails steps 3 and 4 and is `log-signature`: every other body fault here is signed by the log, so it is the one that holds the order between them. `checkpoints-bad/24-log-key-other-algorithm-length` and `checkpoints-bad/28-witness-key-other-algorithm-length` each add a line of the other supported length under a matched key — the log's and a listed witness's — and are refused as `log-signature` and `cosignature`, never skipped. **Start here if you are checking your verifier**: `04`, `08`, `11`, `12` and `16` are the files in the suite that a verifier which never checks a note or cosignature signature will accept — `cases.json` lists them under `signature_blind_accepts`, so the two cannot drift apart |
| `proofs/` | one self-contained bundle per proven device (§8), plus `at-the-cap.bundle`: the valid `nas` bundle grown to exactly 81919 bytes (`MAX_BUNDLE_BYTES`) with real cosignatures from the unlisted `stranger` key, which §10 ignores. It MUST be accepted; `cases.json` names it under `at_the_cap`. Decode bundles with the 81919-byte bundle limit, not the default 65535-byte entry limit. Also `right-edge.json`: the last-leaf inclusion proof at index 126 in a 127-entry tree, with its entry, root and proof hashes. `cases.json` records the checkpoint time under the policy that accepted it and the counterfactual time under the policy replayed from it |
| `proofs-bad/` | thirteen bundles that MUST be refused (§8): `one-past-the-cap` is the positive cap bundle grown by one byte to 81920, otherwise sound and refused as `bundle` on length; a wrong entry, a foreign checkpoint, a tampered proof, a checkpoint signed by a key the anchor does not name, one with no witness quorum and one whose checkpoint names another origin. `cases.json` gives the log key, what each refusal must be about, and in `codes` the SPEC §10.1 code each MUST be refused with. Three fail two steps and are coded with the earlier one, which is how §10.1's bundle order is checkable: `foreign-checkpoint` is `log-signature` and not `origin`, `wrong-entry` is `inclusion` and not `binding`, and `no-quorum-tampered-proof` — no cosignature and a tampered proof — is `quorum` and not `inclusion`. `rotate-entry-other-device` and `revoke-entry-other-device` prove a `rotate` and a `revoke` under another device's label (`binding`): §8.1 binds those through the body's `device_id`, not an embedded request |
| `detect/` | **pairs**, not single artifacts: a checkpoint the reader already holds and one it is then offered, each branch served with its own tiles. Accepting a grown head, refusing a shrunk one *without* calling it a fork, and proving a fork from either side — at the same size, on a shorter branch, and on a longer one (`fork-on-a-longer-branch`). `cases.json`'s `codes` names the SPEC §10.1 code for every case that is not accepted; `tampered-bundle-under-a-stored-head` is this log with one corrupt byte, and it is `head`, **not** `fork` — the head is checked before the branches are compared, so one bad byte in transit is never an accusation. `staleness.json` is §8.1 condition 4's ladder as a table, read top to bottom: the two cases with `hard` 700 under `staleness` 900 sit where `fresh` and `hard_stale` can both hold, and `hard_stale` wins (D-060) — `hard-below-staleness` is `hard_stale` at 800 seconds, and `at-the-hard-boundary` is still `fresh` at exactly 700, because the limit is a strict `>` |
| `served-rotated/` | the served head signed by a key the roots published in the log (§9.4). The only vector with two correct answers: refuse it holding only `trust.cbor`, accept it having replayed this log |
| `served-extra-witness/` | the served head plus one more cosignature line, from a witness the policy never names. It MUST be **accepted**: an unknown line is ignored, not refused, because a witness cosigning a log this node does not list is normal in a shared log. Serve it over `served/`'s tiles |
| `served-name-collision/` | the served head plus one more line carrying a **listed** witness's name under a key the policy does not publish for it — the same key `served-extra-witness/` uses, under a borrowed name. §7 makes the key id bind the name, so the line names nobody: it MUST be **accepted**, ignored exactly like a stranger's. Two lines carry the name and one carries the key id. A reader matching on the name alone refuses this head, which would let anyone deny a checkpoint to every node on the network by cosigning it under a name they do not hold. Serve it over `served/`'s tiles |
| `served-twice-cosigned/` | the served head where one witness answers **twice** and both lines verify. It MUST be accepted; `cases.json` gives the evaluation time §5.3's tie-break produces, and the one an oldest-line reader would get instead. Serve it over `served/`'s tiles |
| `served-superseded/` | the served head cosigned by two of three witnesses: accepted by a reader holding only `trust.cbor`, refused by one that has replayed the roots raising the quorum (§9.4) |
| `served-large/` | a Go-generated, signed 300-entry log with a full level-0 tile, a partial level-0 tile, and a level-1 tile; `cases.json` records every implied tile path and width |
| `served-bad/` | §6's refusals over an honest copy of `served-large/`: a tampered entry bundle, a missing one, a tampered hash tile, a missing one, a missing checkpoint, a log tampered **consistently**, and an over-full final bundle. `consistent-tampered-log` changes the entries and level-0 tile together, so only rebuilding and comparing the head can refuse it. The over-full bundle decodes but carries one more entry than the size and path imply. `cases.json`'s `codes` names the §10.1 code each MUST be refused with, and §10.1 compares the head **before** it opens a tile: `tampered-entry-bundle` fails both head and tiles, and is `head` — a reader that checks tiles first, or never rebuilds the tree, answers `tiles`. Each case names the path to replace with `file`, paths to replace with `files`, or path to delete with `remove` |
| `fork/` | `evidence.cbor` and `conflicting.checkpoint`: a second branch of this same network, proving the evidence format (§11.1) is checkable by anybody holding `trust.cbor` — plus twenty-two that must be **refused**, at least one for every SPEC §11.1 code: `bad-oversize`, `bad-oversize-and-not-cbor` and `bad-one-past-the-cap` — sound evidence exactly one byte past `MAX_EVIDENCE_BYTES` — (`oversize`); `bad-non-canonical-cbor` (`cbor`) — the sound evidence with `size` written longer than its shortest form, which a reader with a lenient CBOR decoder accepts; `bad-wrong-version` and `bad-version-and-unknown-key` (`version`); `bad-bool-size` (`schema`, true is admitted by CBOR and refused as the wrong `size` type), `bad-open-schema`, `bad-short-held-root-and-size-above-held` and `bad-short-proof-hash` (`schema`); `bad-policy-unparseable` and `bad-policy-unparseable-and-foreign-held` (`policy`); `bad-other-origin` and `bad-policy-says-quorum-none` (`held`); `bad-unverifiable-conflicting` (`conflicting`); `bad-size-above-held` and `bad-size-mismatch` (`size`); `bad-forged-proof`, `bad-proof-at-same-size`, `bad-held-root-at-same-size` (at the held size, a `held_root` that is not the root `held` is signed over — the one comparison there is) and `bad-size-zero` (`proof`); `bad-consistent` (`consistent`). `cases.json`'s `says` is what each refusal must be about, a semantic hint, and its `codes` map names the SPEC §11.1 code each MUST be refused with — the first failing step decides. These five are built to fail more than one step, and are coded with the earliest (others fail more than one incidentally — `bad-open-schema` and `bad-wrong-version` are built on `bad-consistent`): `bad-oversize-and-not-cbor` is `oversize` and not `cbor`, because the size bound is checked before any parse; `bad-other-origin`, wrong in both checkpoints, is `held` and not `conflicting`; `bad-version-and-unknown-key` is `version` and not `schema`, because a key set is only closed relative to a version; `bad-short-held-root-and-size-above-held` is `schema` and not `size`, because a hash's length is part of the schema; `bad-policy-unparseable-and-foreign-held` is `policy` and not `held`, because the unparseable carried policy is step 4 and the foreign held checkpoint is step 5. `cases.json`'s `sound` names the five files that MUST prove a fork: `evidence`, `policy-not-the-readers`, `evidence-at-64`, `evidence-at-the-cap` (exactly `MAX_EVIDENCE_BYTES` long), and `evidence-at-same-size`. `evidence-at-64` is at a power-of-two size below the held one, the consistency-proof shape RFC 6962 handles with its own branch. `evidence-at-same-size` holds `served/checkpoint` and a conflicting head of the same size with a different root, signed by the log key and cosigned by all three witnesses; its proof is empty and `held_root` is held's signed root. `policy-not-the-readers.cbor` is the positive twin: a carried policy the reader does not share, which MUST still prove the fork |
| `anchors/` | OpenTimestamps proofs, and a calendar's reply, written by `python-opentimestamps`. **Start at `cases.json`**: it gives each proof's digest in hex and names the bytes that produce it, so you can check the rule without parsing the OpenTimestamps container — a format `SPEC.md` does not describe. The checkpoint proof is over `served/checkpoint` **through the newline that terminates the blank separator line** — the three body lines plus the blank line, four `0x0A`. That is not the three-line body and not §7's signed text; anchoring is advisory, so a reader that picks the wrong one of the three never matches a stamp and never says so |

## `SHA256SUMS`

For somebody who downloaded this directory and does not have the generators:
`shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS` from inside it says whether the set is whole and
unmodified. Regenerate with `make vectors-sums` after any change; a test fails
if it is stale.

## Using them

Start at `keys.json` and `entries/`: they need no network, no log and no
crypto beyond Ed25519 and SHA-256. Then `log/manifest.json` and `state.json`,
which together are §5's replay in one comparison. `served/` and `proofs/` need
a `tlog-tiles` reader. `trust-bad/`, `requests-bad/` and `log/*.reason` are the
half most implementations get wrong: each is a file that **must be refused**,
and for the stated reason.

**`cases.json`'''s `says` field is a semantic hint**, not the bytes your
implementation must produce. §5.2 gives replay a closed list of reason codes and
no other layer has one, so outside replay there is nothing to compare: map each
`says` onto your own error by hand, once. What it is for is the discipline it
enforces here — a negative must be refused for its own rule and nothing else,
and a phrase naming that rule is how the generators check it.

A file being absent from this list is a bug in the list — a test in
`internal/specdoc` fails if anything here is undescribed.
